title: Near-death experiences
hook: many report light and peace, and scientists and traditions read these very differently

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Cicely Saunders, and what hospice staff see at the bedside. Your line was a gradual winding down. Today, people who came close to death and came back with a story.

A man's heart stops on an operating table. The team works on him, and he comes back. Days later, still shaky, he tries to tell his wife something and can't find the words. He says he felt calm, calmer than he's ever been. There was light, and he didn't want to leave it. He's a little embarrassed. He also says he isn't afraid of dying anymore. Doctors and researchers have collected accounts like his, from people of different backgrounds. They're called near-death experiences.

The accounts vary, but certain things come up again and again: a deep peace, a sense of leaving the body, a light, sometimes meeting people who have died, sometimes a review of one's life, and a point of return. Not everyone has all of these, and some accounts are frightening rather than peaceful. One psychiatrist who has long collected these accounts has written that people often come back less afraid of death and more concerned with love and meaning. Whatever the experience is, it seems to leave a mark. Some scientists look to the brain under extreme stress: a lack of oxygen, chemical changes, the dreaming parts of the brain breaking into waking. On this reading, the experience is real as an experience, and the brain is producing it. Researchers who hold this view point out that similar sensations can show up in other situations where the brain is under strain. Some people in religious traditions, and some researchers, read these accounts as glimpses of something beyond the body, a sign that consciousness may not end where the brain does. They point to people describing events in the room while they seemed unconscious, and say the brain explanation doesn't yet cover everything. So here is where it stands: the experiences are reported, and what they mean is argued over by careful people on more than one side. It's allowed to stay open.
screen: `PEACE, LIGHT, RETURN.` · `LESS AFRAID AFTERWARD.` · `READING ONE: THE BRAIN.` · `READING TWO: BEYOND IT.` · then, large: `NOT SETTLED.`

segments.voice: Picture the man from the operating table telling his story, and hear it first as a brain doing something remarkable under strain, then as a glimpse of something beyond. Let both sit side by side, the way two cups sit on one table, and notice which one you lean toward, and that you don't have to decide right now.
Near-death experiences: accounts of peace, light and leaving the body from people who came close to death, read by some as the brain at work and by others as a glimpse beyond. Today's word.
Your line: not settled. Careful people still disagree about it, and that's all right. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Researchers in medicine and psychology collect and study near-death accounts, and people in religious traditions talk about them in light of their own teachings about death and the soul.
